::: {.callout-note .se-question appearance="simple"}
## The question

[Trouble with L'Hopitals rule when calculating $\lim_{x\to2\pm\sqrt3}\frac{e^{-x}}{-x^2+4x-1}$](https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/4705640/trouble-with-lhopitals-rule-when-calculating-lim-x-to2-pm-sqrt3-frace-x), asked by [user1184477](https://math.stackexchange.com/users/1184477/user1184477) on Mathematics Stack Exchange (2023-05-24; [CC BY-SA 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/)):

> I was asked to find the limit of $$\frac{e^{-x}}{-x^2+4x-1}$$ as $x$ tends to $2 + \sqrt{3}$ and $2 - \sqrt{3}$.
>
> I tried to use L'Hôpital's rule as the denominator would otherwise be $0$. After differentiating twice, I got $\frac{e^{-x}}{-2}$. However, when I take the limits, I get a value, which is incorrect as I can see from the graph of the function that the limit is $+\infty$ or $-\infty$. I would really appreciate if someone could explain to me what I am doing wrong here. Thank you!
:::

This is a good question. You're basically saying, *my eyes tell me one thing (from the graph), but L'Hopital's rule tells me another. What am I missing?*

The answer, as I said in my comment, is that you're missing one of the hypotheses of L'Hopital's rule. It is not sufficient that the denominator tend to zero; both the numerator and denominator must tend to zero in order to substitute the limit of the quotient of the derivatives. So L'Hopital is out of the question here.

The graph shows you that there are vertical asymptotes at the two zeros of the denominator, with limits of $\pm\infty$ on each side. To verify this rigorously, it's hard to find the right balance between manual dexterity (i.e., hand waving), and epsilon-delta. As an instructor, I would be looking for something like this: As $x\to (2-\sqrt{3})^-$, the numerator tends to a positive number, while the denominator tends to zero but remains positive. So the limit from the left is $+\infty$. And so on.
